table.header: Is a joke funnier if it is told by a man? A novel paradigm using AI-generated voices

table.text: Out of the valid responses, 535 identified as female, 396 as male, 31 as non-binary/third gender, and 4 preferred not to disclose their gender. 597 participants were recruited from Prolific and compensated approximately $1.25 AUD for completing a 5-minute survey.

Another 135 participants were from the [hidden] first-year participant pool and were awarded 0.5 research credits for their participation. 234 participants were recruited using flyers placed around the University of Queensland campus, through Reddit, or Facebook.

The sexual orientations of participants were diverse: 719 identified as heterosexual/straight, 48 as gay/lesbian, 144 as bisexual, 28 selected an option not listed, and 27 preferred not to say or did not respond.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of the four conditions, ensuring that each condition had an approximately equal number of participants across the gender categories.
After participants answered demographic questions, participants were randomly assigned into one of the four voice conditions.
To avoid any implicit cues about the true purpose of the study, all audio presented was consistent with the voice condition that participants were assigned to.
Participants were then presented with each of the 12 jokes in random order and asked to rate each joke on a scale of 1 to 7 (1 = not funny at all,3 = a little funny,5 = pretty funny,7 = very funny).

After all jokes had been rated, participants were asked to listen to a neutral statement spoken by their assigned voice: "I never have trouble sleeping when there's a storm because the sound of rain helps me to fall asleep."

Participants were asked to rate their agreement (1 = strongly disagree to7 = strongly agree) on statements starting with, "Their voice sounded…" on the following traits: "attractive", "confident", "warm", "competent", "charismatic", and "masculine".

Participants were then asked to choose the statement that they agreed with: "Men are funnier than women", "Men and women are equally funny", or "Women are funnier than men", and to select which of the following statements were true about themselves: "I have more male friends than female friends", "I have an equal number of male and female friends", or "I have more female friends than male friends".
We note that only male and female participants were retained in these analyses due to insufficient sample size in the other gender categories.

The age of our participants did not explain our observed discrepancies; neither participant age (p = .186) nor an interaction between participant age and gender were associated with agreement of "being funny is a masculine trait" (p ≥ .227).
There was also no difference in these attitudes across our three recruitment sources (SONA, Prolific, word of mouth) (p = .128).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: In our main preregistered analysis, we investigated whether there was a main effect of the apparent gender of the voice on funniness ratings, i.e. Are jokes told by a male voice funnier than jokes told by a female voice? While controlling for participant gender, an interaction between the gender of the participant, the apparent gender of the voice, and the gender of the original voice, we found no significant difference in the funniness ratings of jokes told by apparently male and female voices, γ(SE) = -0.03(0.08), t(942.20)= -0.32, p = .745, 95% CI = [-0.19, 0.13]. A sensitivity power analysisfoot_0 revealed that 0.012 was the minimum effect size that could be detected with 80% power given a sample size of n = 966.
G*Power was used to determine Cohen's F 2 for a multiple linear regression (fixed model, R² deviation from zero).

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Perceptions of humour
table.research_questions:
Hypothesis 1: 
We expect a main effect of the apparent gender of the speaker on funniness. Specifically, we expect that the mean funniness rating for jokes delivered with a male voice will be higher than ratings of jokes delivered by a female voice. We expect this effect will be present even when controlling for the gender of the rater, as well as the gender of the original speaker (this is to account for speaking differences/cadence/delivery in the original AI voices).
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
table.randomization: Participants will be randomly allocated experimental conditions (male or female voice). We aim to achieve roughly equal numbers of male and female participants for each experimental condition.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures:
We are looking to recruit participants only of ages 18 and over. Participants must regard English as their first language and must have normal hearing. Data will be collected online. Participants will be either recruited from Prolific, the UQ SONA system (to recruit first year psychology students), and through word of mouth (via flyers, Facebook groups, Reddit). 

We are aiming to collect at least 930 participants. We have enough funds (800 AUD) to collect 630 participants from Prolific for a five minute study. And we are hoping for at least 200 participants from the UQ SONA system. We are also hoping to recruit about 100 participants through flyers/Facebook groups/Reddit. We will aim to keep data collection open for the first 4 weeks of Semester 2 (until the 19th of August). We will stop all data collection on the 19th of August.
table.sample_size: We aim to have at least 930 participants (465 males, 465 females). We do not have a strict limit, but we will stop collecting data on the 19th of August.
table.sample_size_rationale: The sample size is based on time and money constraints. As mentioned above, we have enough money to collect 630 participants from Prolific. And we are aiming to use first year psychology students as participants, so we are limited by the academic calendar, as we are unable to collect student data over the winter break.
table.stopping_rule: We will stop recruiting on the 19th of August.
table.indices: We will treat each joke rating as an observation. Since participants are rating the same 12 jokes, we will use multilevel modelling to account for any variance that is attributed to any single joke (e.g. one joke could be on average funnier than another joke), so we will use the joke ID as a random intercept. In addition, the joke rating is dependent on the participant who gave the rating, so we will also control for this using a random intercept for each participant. We will also include random intercepts for the sample type (Prolific, UQ SONA, and word of mouth), nationality, ethnicity, and sexual orientation.
table.statistical_tests:
Hypothesis 1:
We will use a multilevel model, where the outcome variable is the joke rating. The predictors will be the interaction between participant gender (male, female) x apparent gender of the speaker (male, female) while controlling for the true gender of the speaker (male, female). Random intercepts for the joke ID, the participant ID, and the sample type (Prolific, UQ SONA, and word of mouth), nationality, ethnicity, and sexual orientation will be added. 
If an interaction between apparent gender and participant gender exists, we will follow this up to determine the nature of the interaction. We will calculate estimated marginal means and perform pairwise comparisons.
table.inference_criteria: We will use p values with a cut off criteria of 0.05. We will be using two tailed tests for each of our analyses.
table.missing_data_handling: Each response is compulsory, so the participant will not be able to move on with the survey without selecting an option. If a participant does not complete the survey, we will not include the participant in our analyses.
table.exploratory_analyses:
Additional exploratory analyses:

We will also use a multilevel model to investigate whether a three way interaction exists between participant gender (male, female) x apparent gender of the speaker(male, female) x and gender funniness attitude (men are funnier than females, men and women are equally funny, women are funnier than men) on the outcome of funniness ratings, we also control for the true gender of the speaker (male, female). If this interaction is significant, we will use follow up tests to further investigate the nature of the interaction. We intend to include random intercepts for the joke ID, the participant ID, and the sample type (Prolific, UQ SONA, and word of mouth), nationality, ethnicity, and sexual orientation.

We also plan to use a multilevel model to investigate whether a three way interaction exists between participant gender (male, female) x apparent gender of the speaker (male, female) x and gender friendship proportion (I have more male friends than female friends, I have an equal number of male and female friends, I have more female friends than male friends) on the outcome of funniness ratings, we also control for the true gender of the speaker (male, female). If this interaction is significant, we will use follow up tests to further investigate the nature of the interaction. We intend to include random intercepts for the joke ID, the participant ID, and the sample type (Prolific, UQ SONA, and word of mouth), nationality, ethnicity, and sexual orientation.

We also plan to use a multilevel model to investigate whether a three way interaction exists between participant gender (male, female) x apparent gender of the speaker (male, female) x and gender friendship proportion (I have more male friends than female friends, I have an equal number of male and female friends, I have more female friends than male friends) on the outcome of funniness ratings, we also control for the true gender of the speaker (male, female). If this interaction is significant, we will use follow up tests to further investigate the nature of the interaction. We intend to include random intercepts for the joke ID, the participant ID, and the sample type (Prolific, UQ SONA, and word of mouth), nationality, ethnicity, and sexual orientation.

We will also assess whether there were inherent differences between voices that were  transformed (male to female/female to male) and voices that were not transformed (Originally voiced by Chris/ originally voiced by Rachel). Participants who are assigned to the female voice condition will hear a voice speaking a neutral statement that is originally female (voiced by Rachel) or male transformed to female (voiced by Chris and transformed into Rachel). And participants in the male voice condition will hear the same neutral statement that is spoken by a voice that is originally male (voiced by Chris) or female transformed to male (voiced by Rachel and transformed into Chris). We ask participants to rate on a scale of 1 to 7 (strongly disagree to strongly agree) how attractive, confident, warm, competent, and charismatic the voice sounds. And we will assess if there are any differences between the original and transformed voices for each voice gender. These analyses will involve:
-	2 way ANOVA with the variable female voice type (originally female, male transformed to female) and controlling for participant gender (female, male) on the voice ratings for the traits “attractive”, “confident”, “warm”, “competent”, and “charismatic” (this ANOVA will be conducted for each of these outcome variables)
-	2 way ANOVA with the variable male voice type (originally male, female transformed to male) and controlling for participant gender (female, male) on the voice ratings for the traits “attractive”, “confident”, “warm”, “competent”, and “charismatic” (this ANOVA will be conducted for each of these outcome variables)

We also want to investigate whether gender funniness attitude (i.e. Men are funnier than women, Men and women are equally funny, Women are funnier than men) predicts the extent that one agrees with this statement "Being funny is a masculine trait". This will be done using a one way ANOVA. Follow up tests will be conducted if there is a significant main effect of gender funniness attitude. 

We also investigate whether the predominant gender of a participants' friends associate with gendered attitudes toward humour. This will be done with a one way ANOVA of friend gender (3 levels: more male friends than female, equal number of male and female friends, and more female friends than male) on the DV "Being funny is a masculine trait".
We also want to look at whether friend gender is associated with gendered funniness attitudes (i.e. Men are funnier than women/Men and women are equally funny/Women are funnier than men). A chi square test will be used to investigate this.
table.q5: From the information sheet and study advertisement, it should not be clear to the participant that we are interested in investigating the gender effects of the speaker. And it should not be clear that we are also transforming the apparent gender of the speaker of the jokes. In the sign up information, we are framing it as a joke rating study.
table.study_design_overview:
This will be a between groups design (2x2). Each participant will be randomly assigned into one of four groups:
- listen to a male voice 
- listen to audio originally delivered by a female and transformed into a male's voice
- listen to a female voice 
- listen to audio originally delivered by a male and transformed into a female's voice
table.manipulated_variables:
Apparent gender of the speaker:
This describes the apparent gender of the voice that participants will listen to. We randomly assign each participant to listen to a male or a female voice. 

True gender of the speaker:
The true gender of the speaker describes the original (untransformed) gender of the voice that delivered the joke. This would be male or female. 

We use two voices on Elevenlabs (elevenlabs.io), Chris and Matilda. In total there are 12 jokes. All of which have been replicated under the four experimental conditions.

After each joke we will ask:
How funny was the joke?
•	1 = not at all funny
•	3 = a little funny
•	5 = pretty funny
•	7 = very funny

We then ask the participant to evaluate the voice that they have been listening to (either an original voice or a transformed voice says a neutral statement):
Participants will rate on a scale of 1= Strongly disagree, 4= Neutral, 7= Strongly agree on the following statements:
Their voice sounded attractive
Their voice sounded confident
Their voice sounded warm
Their voice sounded competent
Their voice sounded charismatic

We will then ask participants for their attitudes using the same 1-7 scale as above.
I am funny
I find other people funny
I prefer a partner who makes me laugh
I prefer a partner who laughs at my humour
Being funny is a masculine trait

We also ask them which statement they agree with:
Which statement do you agree with? 
•	Men are funnier than women
•	Men and women are equally funny
•	Women are funnier than men

and
Which of the following statements is true about yourself?
•	I have more male friends than female friends
•	I have an equal number of male and female friends
•	I have more female friends than male friends
table.data_exclusion_criteria: We will be conducting attention checks. There are 2 attention checks included in the survey which ask about the content of the joke. Participants who fail both attention checks will be excluded from the dataset.

table.missing_data_handling: Each response is compulsory, so the participant will not be able to move on with the survey without selecting an option. If a participant does not complete the survey, we will not include the participant in our analyses.
table.exploratory_analyses:
Additional exploratory analyses:

We will also use a multilevel model to investigate whether a three way interaction exists between participant gender (male, female) x apparent gender of the speaker(male, female) x and gender funniness attitude (men are funnier than females, men and women are equally funny, women are funnier than men) on the outcome of funniness ratings, we also control for the true gender of the speaker (male, female). If this interaction is significant, we will use follow up tests to further investigate the nature of the interaction. We intend to include random intercepts for the joke ID, the participant ID, and the sample type (Prolific, UQ SONA, and word of mouth), nationality, ethnicity, and sexual orientation.

We also plan to use a multilevel model to investigate whether a three way interaction exists between participant gender (male, female) x apparent gender of the speaker (male, female) x and gender friendship proportion (I have more male friends than female friends, I have an equal number of male and female friends, I have more female friends than male friends) on the outcome of funniness ratings, we also control for the true gender of the speaker (male, female). If this interaction is significant, we will use follow up tests to further investigate the nature of the interaction. We intend to include random intercepts for the joke ID, the participant ID, and the sample type (Prolific, UQ SONA, and word of mouth), nationality, ethnicity, and sexual orientation.

We also plan to use a multilevel model to investigate whether a three way interaction exists between participant gender (male, female) x apparent gender of the speaker (male, female) x and gender friendship proportion (I have more male friends than female friends, I have an equal number of male and female friends, I have more female friends than male friends) on the outcome of funniness ratings, we also control for the true gender of the speaker (male, female). If this interaction is significant, we will use follow up tests to further investigate the nature of the interaction. We intend to include random intercepts for the joke ID, the participant ID, and the sample type (Prolific, UQ SONA, and word of mouth), nationality, ethnicity, and sexual orientation.

We will also assess whether there were inherent differences between voices that were  transformed (male to female/female to male) and voices that were not transformed (Originally voiced by Chris/ originally voiced by Rachel). Participants who are assigned to the female voice condition will hear a voice speaking a neutral statement that is originally female (voiced by Rachel) or male transformed to female (voiced by Chris and transformed into Rachel). And participants in the male voice condition will hear the same neutral statement that is spoken by a voice that is originally male (voiced by Chris) or female transformed to male (voiced by Rachel and transformed into Chris). We ask participants to rate on a scale of 1 to 7 (strongly disagree to strongly agree) how attractive, confident, warm, competent, and charismatic the voice sounds. And we will assess if there are any differences between the original and transformed voices for each voice gender. These analyses will involve:
-	2 way ANOVA with the variable female voice type (originally female, male transformed to female) and controlling for participant gender (female, male) on the voice ratings for the traits “attractive”, “confident”, “warm”, “competent”, and “charismatic” (this ANOVA will be conducted for each of these outcome variables)
-	2 way ANOVA with the variable male voice type (originally male, female transformed to male) and controlling for participant gender (female, male) on the voice ratings for the traits “attractive”, “confident”, “warm”, “competent”, and “charismatic” (this ANOVA will be conducted for each of these outcome variables)

We also want to investigate whether gender funniness attitude (i.e. Men are funnier than women, Men and women are equally funny, Women are funnier than men) predicts the extent that one agrees with this statement "Being funny is a masculine trait". This will be done using a one way ANOVA. Follow up tests will be conducted if there is a significant main effect of gender funniness attitude. 

We also investigate whether the predominant gender of a participants' friends associate with gendered attitudes toward humour. This will be done with a one way ANOVA of friend gender (3 levels: more male friends than female, equal number of male and female friends, and more female friends than male) on the DV "Being funny is a masculine trait".
We also want to look at whether friend gender is associated with gendered funniness attitudes (i.e. Men are funnier than women/Men and women are equally funny/Women are funnier than men). A chi square test will be used to investigate this.
table.q5: From the information sheet and study advertisement, it should not be clear to the participant that we are interested in investigating the gender effects of the speaker. And it should not be clear that we are also transforming the apparent gender of the speaker of the jokes. In the sign up information, we are framing it as a joke rating study.
table.study_design_overview:
This will be a between groups design (2x2). Each participant will be randomly assigned into one of four groups:
- listen to a male voice 
- listen to audio originally delivered by a female and transformed into a male's voice
- listen to a female voice 
- listen to audio originally delivered by a male and transformed into a female's voice
table.manipulated_variables:
Apparent gender of the speaker:
This describes the apparent gender of the voice that participants will listen to. We randomly assign each participant to listen to a male or a female voice. 

True gender of the speaker:
The true gender of the speaker describes the original (untransformed) gender of the voice that delivered the joke. This would be male or female. 

We use two voices on Elevenlabs (elevenlabs.io), Chris and Matilda. In total there are 12 jokes. All of which have been replicated under the four experimental conditions.

stat_check.summary_text: We detected no errors in t-tests or F-tests.

table.text: While controlling for participant gender, an interaction between the gender of the participant, the apparent gender of the voice, and the gender of the original voice, we found no significant difference in the funniness ratings of jokes told by apparently male and female voices, γ(SE) = -0.03(0.08), t(942.20)= -0.32, p = .745, 95% CI = [-0.19, 0.13].

We found no evidence of such an interaction between the gender of the participant and the apparent gender of the voice on ratings of funniness (γ(SE) = -0.06(0.13), t(941.93)= -0.49, p = .622, 95% CI = [-0.31, 0.19]).
We also found no evidence of a difference in funniness when jokes were originally voiced by a male or female AI voice, γ(SE) = -0.02(0.06), t(938.73)= -0.30, p = .762, 95% CI = [-0.14, 0.10].
We found that on average, men rated jokes 0.39 units (out of 7) funnier than women, γ(SE) = 0.39(0.09), t(945.52)= 4.23, p < .001, 95% CI = [0.21, 0.57].

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 1 data file could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: In contrast, Mickes et al. (2012) found no difference in the actual funniness of men's and women's cartoon captions in one study, despite strong beliefs that men were funnier. Caldwell and Wojtach (2019) further showed that humour self-efficacy mattered: when participants completed an easy practice task intended to increase confidence, women's captions were rated funnier than men's; when the practice task was difficult and presumably lowered confidence, men's captions were rated funnier.

Out of the valid responses, 535 identified as female, 396 as male, 31 as non-binary/third gender, and 4 preferred not to disclose their gender. 597 participants were recruited from Prolific and compensated approximately $1.25 AUD for completing a 5-minute survey.

Another 135 participants were from the [hidden] first-year participant pool and were awarded 0.5 research credits for their participation. 234 participants were recruited using flyers placed around the University of Queensland campus, through Reddit, or Facebook.

The sexual orientations of participants were diverse: 719 identified as heterosexual/straight, 48 as gay/lesbian, 144 as bisexual, 28 selected an option not listed, and 27 preferred not to say or did not respond.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of the four conditions, ensuring that each condition had an approximately equal number of participants across the gender categories.
After participants answered demographic questions, participants were randomly assigned into one of the four voice conditions.
To avoid any implicit cues about the true purpose of the study, all audio presented was consistent with the voice condition that participants were assigned to.
Participants were then presented with each of the 12 jokes in random order and asked to rate each joke on a scale of 1 to 7 (1 = not funny at all,3 = a little funny,5 = pretty funny,7 = very funny).

After all jokes had been rated, participants were asked to listen to a neutral statement spoken by their assigned voice: "I never have trouble sleeping when there's a storm because the sound of rain helps me to fall asleep."

Participants were asked to rate their agreement (1 = strongly disagree to7 = strongly agree) on statements starting with, "Their voice sounded…" on the following traits: "attractive", "confident", "warm", "competent", "charismatic", and "masculine".

Participants were then asked to choose the statement that they agreed with: "Men are funnier than women", "Men and women are equally funny", or "Women are funnier than men", and to select which of the following statements were true about themselves: "I have more male friends than female friends", "I have an equal number of male and female friends", or "I have more female friends than male friends".
We note that only male and female participants were retained in these analyses due to insufficient sample size in the other gender categories.

The age of our participants did not explain our observed discrepancies; neither participant age (p = .186) nor an interaction between participant age and gender were associated with agreement of "being funny is a masculine trait" (p ≥ .227).
There was also no difference in these attitudes across our three recruitment sources (SONA, Prolific, word of mouth) (p = .128).

info.title: Is a joke funnier if it is told by a man? A novel paradigm using AI-generated voices

text.text: The stereotype that "men are funnier than women" is culturally pervasive.
In a large preregistered online study (n=966), participants rated 12 jokes delivered by a male or female AI-generated voice.
To control for differences in delivery, cadence, and intonation, we used a speech-to-speech transformation to transform jokes spoken by a female into a male version and vice versa.
Using a Bayesian analysis, we found strong evidence that the apparent gender of the speaker does not affect the perceived funniness of the joke (BF=0.023).

We found no interaction between the original and apparent voice gender on masculinity ratings, indicating that vocal gender cues were effectively eliminated when voices were transformed to the opposite gender, reinforcing the merit of this gender manipulation method.

Further, men had significantly higher agreement that being funny is a masculine trait than women (M D =0.73, p adj <.001), and participants with more male than female friends had significantly higher agreement with this belief than those with equal numbers of male and female friends (M D =0.68, p adj <.001) or more female than male friends (M D =0.91, p adj <.001).
text.formatted: Further, men had significantly higher agreement that being funny is a masculine trait than women (M D =0.73, p adj <.001), and participants with more male than female friends had significantly higher agreement with this belief than those with equal numbers of male and female friends (M D =0.68, p adj <.001) or more female than male friends (M D =0.91, p adj <.001).

text.text: In all, apparent vocal gender does not appear to influence humour evaluations directly, but exploratory findings suggest the apparent vocal gender and delivery may shape broader impressions of speakers (such as perceived confidence and charisma).
And individual differences such as gender and proportion of male friends may shape gendered attitudes and expectations toward humour.
The stereotype that "men are funnier than women" is widespread in both popular media (e.g. Hitchens, 2007) and in lay beliefs held by men and women (Hooper et al., 2016; Mickes et al., 2012).
text.formatted: The stereotype that "men are funnier than women" is widespread in both popular media (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Hitchens, 2007)</ref> and in lay beliefs held by men and women <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hooper et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Mickes et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: For example, men are more commonly identified as the funnier gender, and funny cartoon captions are more likely to attributed to male authors, while unfunny captions are attributed to female authors (Hooper et al., 2016; Mickes et al., 2012).
text.formatted: For example, men are more commonly identified as the funnier gender, and funny cartoon captions are more likely to attributed to male authors, while unfunny captions are attributed to female authors <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hooper et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Mickes et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This raises an important question: does this stereotype reflect genuine gender differences in humour production, or does it partly arise because equivalent humour is evaluated differently when it is believed to come from a man rather than a woman?
These possibilities are not mutually exclusive.
Humour is inherently evaluative: a joke is funny only to the extent that an audience finds it funny.
However, evaluations may reflect more than the content of a joke and the quality of its delivery.
They may also be shaped by assumptions about the speaker.

If men are expected to be witty, confident, intelligent, or socially dominant, while women are expected to be less humorous or face greater social costs for performing humour, identical material may be interpreted differently depending on the perceived gender of its source.
This possibility is especially important because humour can signal socially valued traits, including competence, status, creativity, and affiliation (Bear & Miron-Spektor, 2024).
text.formatted: This possibility is especially important because humour can signal socially valued traits, including competence, status, creativity, and affiliation <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bear & Miron-Spektor, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: One explanation for gendered attitudes towards humour comes from evolutionary theory.
Humour production, along with language, has been proposed as an indicator of cognitive fitness (Greengross & Miller, 2011; Miller, 2001; Miller, 2006).
text.formatted: Humour production, along with language, has been proposed as an indicator of cognitive fitness <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Greengross & Miller, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Miller, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Miller, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, humour and other cognitively demanding displays may have evolved through mutual mate choice as signals of underlying mate quality.
Sexual selection theory further predicts greater female selectivity in mate choice given women's greater minimum reproductive costs (Trivers, 1972).
text.formatted: Sexual selection theory further predicts greater female selectivity in mate choice given women's greater minimum reproductive costs <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Trivers, 1972)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with the cognitive fitness indicator theory, women tend to report a preference for humorous partners, whereas men tend to report a preference for partners who appreciate their humour (Bressler et al., 2006; Li et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Consistent with the cognitive fitness indicator theory, women tend to report a preference for humorous partners, whereas men tend to report a preference for partners who appreciate their humour <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bressler et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Li et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: However, evidence from real-life contexts does not show that the attractiveness of humour production or humour receptivity differs reliably by sex (Wainwright et al., 2023).
text.formatted: However, evidence from real-life contexts does not show that the attractiveness of humour production or humour receptivity differs reliably by sex <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Wainwright et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, mate-preference findings alone do not establish that men are inherently funnier, nor do they explain why people may systematically credit men more readily for humour.

A contrasting explanation is provided by social role theory, which proposes that gender differences in behaviour and beliefs partly reflect the historically unequal social roles occupied by men and women (Eagly & Wood, 2012).
text.formatted: A contrasting explanation is provided by social role theory, which proposes that gender differences in behaviour and beliefs partly reflect the historically unequal social roles occupied by men and women <ref type="bibr">(Eagly & Wood, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Because men have traditionally occupied more positions of economic and social power, gender stereotypes may associate men with traits considered useful for high-status roles, such as assertiveness, confidence, and competence.
Humour may become gendered when it is culturally associated with these traits.

Expectations that men should be funny may then influence both behaviour and evaluation: men may be more encouraged to attempt humour, and in turn, audiences may be more likely to recognise, reward, and remember humour when it is attributed to men.
Although gendered expectations may shape both the expression and reception of humour, much existing research has examined whether men and women differ in their ability to produce humour.
A meta-analysis by Greengross et al. (2020), including 5,057 participants, reported a small-to-moderate average difference favouring men in humourproduction ability, with an effect size of d = 0.32.
text.formatted: A meta-analysis by <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Greengross et al. (2020)</ref>, including 5,057 participants, reported a small-to-moderate average difference favouring men in humourproduction ability, with an effect size of d = 0.32.

text.text: Across the evaluated studies, men's humorous output was rated as funnier than women's even when judges were unaware of the producer's gender.

However, most studies assessed humour with constrained laboratory tasks, particularly cartoon-caption writing tasks analogous to the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest (e.g. Feingold & Mazzella, 1993; Greengross & Miller, 2011).
text.formatted: However, most studies assessed humour with constrained laboratory tasks, particularly cartoon-caption writing tasks analogous to the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Feingold & Mazzella, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Greengross & Miller, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Other paradigms have included completing a humorous résumé (Howrigan & MacDonald, 2008), generating funny responses to unusual prompts, and joke-completion tasks (Nusbaum et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Other paradigms have included completing a humorous résumé <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Howrigan & MacDonald, 2008)</ref>, generating funny responses to unusual prompts, and joke-completion tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Nusbaum et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Although some of these measures correlate with cartoon-caption performance, they require specific written, visual, and contextual skills and may not adequately represent the spontaneous and socially embedded humour of everyday interaction.

Research also suggests that apparent gender differences in humour production can be shaped by factors other than humour ability itself. Silvia et al. (2021) found that women rated their own humour attempts as less funny and expressed lower confidence in their performance than men.
text.formatted: Research also suggests that apparent gender differences in humour production can be shaped by factors other than humour ability itself. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Silvia et al. (2021)</ref> found that women rated their own humour attempts as less funny and expressed lower confidence in their performance than men.

text.text: In contrast, Mickes et al. (2012) found no difference in the actual funniness of men's and women's cartoon captions in one study, despite strong beliefs that men were funnier. Caldwell and Wojtach (2019) further showed that humour self-efficacy mattered: when participants completed an easy practice task intended to increase confidence, women's captions were rated funnier than men's; when the practice task was difficult and presumably lowered confidence, men's captions were rated funnier.
text.formatted: In contrast, <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Mickes et al. (2012)</ref> found no difference in the actual funniness of men's and women's cartoon captions in one study, despite strong beliefs that men were funnier. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Caldwell and Wojtach (2019)</ref> further showed that humour self-efficacy mattered: when participants completed an easy practice task intended to increase confidence, women's captions were rated funnier than men's; when the practice task was difficult and presumably lowered confidence, men's captions were rated funnier.

text.text: Although men's captions were rated funnier overall in that study, these findings indicate that confidence and task conditions may moderate observed gender differences in constrained humour-production tasks.
Evidence also indicates that gender stereotypes influence humour perception.
In a memory paradigm, Mickes et al. (2012) showed participants cartoon captions that were rated high and low on humour, along with the authors' genders.
text.formatted: In a memory paradigm, <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Mickes et al. (2012)</ref> showed participants cartoon captions that were rated high and low on humour, along with the authors' genders.

text.text: When later asked to recall the author's gender, participants of both genders disproportionately remembered funny captions as male-authored and unfunny captions as female-authored. Hooper et al. (2016) replicated this pattern, supporting the conclusion that people's beliefs about gender can shape whom they credit for humorous material.
text.formatted: When later asked to recall the author's gender, participants of both genders disproportionately remembered funny captions as male-authored and unfunny captions as female-authored. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Hooper et al. (2016)</ref> replicated this pattern, supporting the conclusion that people's beliefs about gender can shape whom they credit for humorous material.

text.text: However, these studies did not test whether the same humorous content is rated as funnier when recipients believe that it was produced by a man rather than a woman.

A small number of studies have manipulated characteristics of humour producers, but none have directly isolated the effect of speaker gender on ratings of spoken joke funniness. Reich et al. (2021), for instance, used written dating vignettes to examine responses to a failed humour attempt by a male or female target.
text.formatted: A small number of studies have manipulated characteristics of humour producers, but none have directly isolated the effect of speaker gender on ratings of spoken joke funniness. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Reich et al. (2021)</ref>, for instance, used written dating vignettes to examine responses to a failed humour attempt by a male or female target.

text.text: The vignettes did not contain humorous material, but participants evaluated the male target's humour mistake as more severe and rated him as less likeable and competent than the female target. Langley and Shiota (2023) used video dating profiles in which male and female confederates gave either humorous or non-humorous responses; humour affected ratings of targets, but speaker gender was not the central experimental question.
text.formatted: The vignettes did not contain humorous material, but participants evaluated the male target's humour mistake as more severe and rated him as less likeable and competent than the female target. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Langley and Shiota (2023)</ref> used video dating profiles in which male and female confederates gave either humorous or non-humorous responses; humour affected ratings of targets, but speaker gender was not the central experimental question.

text.text: Similarly, Yeo et al. (2022) manipulated the gender, race, and professional identity of comedians performing a science-based stand-up routine.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Yeo et al. (2022)</ref> manipulated the gender, race, and professional identity of comedians performing a science-based stand-up routine.

text.text: Although professional comedians were coached to keep pacing, tone, emphasis, and cadence consistent, individual speakers necessarily differed across many vocal dimensions, and humour ratings were not the central outcome.
Most humour in everyday interaction and in media is spoken.
Speech is therefore a crucial context for studying how gendered beliefs about humour may operate.
Yet it presents a methodological challenge: researchers must distinguish a bias in how listeners evaluate men and women from genuine differences in speakers' delivery.

Asking men and women to perform the same jokes does not fully solve this problem, because perceived funniness can depend on subtle features of speech-including cadence, intonation, emphasis, timing, pitch, and timbre-that are difficult to standardise across human speakers (e.g. Langley & Shiota, 2023; Yeo et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Asking men and women to perform the same jokes does not fully solve this problem, because perceived funniness can depend on subtle features of speech-including cadence, intonation, emphasis, timing, pitch, and timbre-that are difficult to standardise across human speakers (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Langley & Shiota, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Yeo et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, an observed difference in ratings could arise from speaker gender, delivery quality, or both.
The present study uses artificial intelligence (AI) to address this limitation.
Specifically, we use AI text-to-speech and speech-to-speech tools to create one-liner jokes in apparently male and female voices.
The stimuli are then gender-transformed, enabling the same underlying vocal delivery and pacing to be presented with either a male or female apparent gender.
By counterbalancing the original AI voice and the direction of gender transformation, the design also controls for differences associated with a particular generated voice or transformation process.
This method makes it possible to test whether identical spoken jokes are judged differently solely because listeners perceive the speaker as male or female.
The study additionally assesses whether the apparent gender of the voice influences evaluations of warmth, charisma, competence, confidence, and attractiveness, using the same design.
And we investigate whether individual differences, such as gender, and proportion of male friends influence gendered attitudes towards humour.
We obtained 1126 responses by our preregistered stopping date.

After excluding participants who were under the age of 18, did not indicate English as a first language, failed attention or comprehension checks, or did not complete the survey, we were left with 966 valid responses (exceeding our preregistered goal of 900).

Out of the valid responses, 535 identified as female, 396 as male, 31 as non-binary/third gender, and 4 preferred not to disclose their gender. 597 participants were recruited from Prolific and compensated approximately $1.25 AUD for completing a 5-minute survey.

Another 135 participants were from the [hidden] first-year participant pool and were awarded 0.5 research credits for their participation. 234 participants were recruited using flyers placed around the University of Queensland campus, through Reddit, or Facebook.
Participant ages ranged from 18 to 78 (M = 29.91, SD = 12.27, median = 26.00).

The sexual orientations of participants were diverse: 719 identified as heterosexual/straight, 48 as gay/lesbian, 144 as bisexual, 28 selected an option not listed, and 27 preferred not to say or did not respond.

Participant ethnicities were also diverse: 9 Aboriginal/Torres Strait Islander, 35 African, 39 African American, 620 Caucasian, 76 East Asian, 22 Latino, 3 Melanesian/Pacific Islander, 15 Middle Eastern, 33 selected an option not listed, 8 preferred not to say.
A majority of participants (91%) were from Western Englishspeaking countries (382 Australia, 176 Canada, 9 New Zealand, 87 United Kingdom, 225 United States of America).
Ethics approval was granted by the Low and Negligible Risk Committee at the University of Queensland (2024/HE000002).
We conducted a 2x2 between-subjects experimental design using an online study.
We manipulated the gender of the originally spoken voice (male or female AI) and the apparent gender of the voice that participants actually hear (male or female).
Participants were randomly assigned to one of the four conditions, ensuring that each condition had an approximately equal number of participants across the gender categories.
We note that we changed the design of our study from a mixed to a between-subjects design out of concern of a confound in the original within-subjects condition.
Details of this change are described in the preregistration (https://osf.io/hu8b4/?view_only=b7cc7a115ef1447e94e859dc468e5441).
text.formatted: Details of this change are described in the preregistration (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/hu8b4/?view_only=b7cc7a115ef1447e94e859dc468e5441">https://osf.io/hu8b4/?view_only=b7cc7a115ef1447e94e859dc468e5441</ref>).

text.text: We initially asked 21 friends and colleagues (7 males, 13 females, and 1 non-binary/third gender) to rate the funniness, offensiveness, and the edginess of 33 one-liner jokes 1 in a survey.
This larger pool of one-liner jokes were selected to be gender-neutral (i.e. could be plausibly delivered by any gender).
From this pool, we selected the funniest-rated jokes provided that fewer than 5 out of 21 respondents rated these as offensive (selected jokes are reported in Table 1).
text.formatted: From this pool, we selected the funniest-rated jokes provided that fewer than 5 out of 21 respondents rated these as offensive (selected jokes are reported in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: 1 Jokes were sourced from joke compilation websites, Reddit, and Youtube.
We used Elevenlabs' text-to-speech and speech-to-speech tools to generate our stimuli (ElevenLabs, 2024).
text.formatted: We used Elevenlabs' text-to-speech and speech-to-speech tools to generate our stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(ElevenLabs, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We chose what we considered to be the most generic female (Matilda) and male voice (Chris) with American accents.
We chose American accents because they are widely familiar in Western society due to the prominence of American media.
We created the original voice stimuli using the text-to-speech tool where the jokes were delivered by Matilda and Chris, respectively.
To enhance humour in delivery, we added punctuation in the text input and used Audacity (Audacity Team, 2022) to edit audio to improve comic timing.
text.formatted: To enhance humour in delivery, we added punctuation in the text input and used Audacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Audacity Team, 2022)</ref> to edit audio to improve comic timing.

text.text: We then created gender-transformed conditions for each original voice using the speech-to-speech tool to transform jokes spoken by Chris to a voice spoken by Matilda or vice versa.
This ensured that the delivery of each joke was maintained across the apparent gender conditions.
We verified the consistency of the joke delivery in the original and transformed conditions using Audacity (see OSF materials).
We advertised a 'Joke Rating Study' aimed at investigating the humorousness of audio jokes and individual attitudes toward humour.
After participants answered demographic questions, participants were randomly assigned into one of the four voice conditions.
We then checked whether participants could listen to and comprehend English audio before beginning the study.
To avoid any implicit cues about the true purpose of the study, all audio presented was consistent with the voice condition that participants were assigned to.
Participants were then presented with each of the 12 jokes in random order and asked to rate each joke on a scale of 1 to 7 (1 = not funny at all,3 = a little funny,5 = pretty funny,7 = very funny).
Two jokes contained comprehension check questions to verify that the participant was listening to the joke.

After all jokes had been rated, participants were asked to listen to a neutral statement spoken by their assigned voice: "I never have trouble sleeping when there's a storm because the sound of rain helps me to fall asleep."

Participants were asked to rate their agreement (1 = strongly disagree to7 = strongly agree) on statements starting with, "Their voice sounded…" on the following traits: "attractive", "confident", "warm", "competent", "charismatic", and "masculine".
The item "Their voice sounded masculine" was included as a manipulation check.

We asked participants to rate themselves (1 = strongly disagree to7 = strongly agree) on the following statements: "I am funny", "I find other people funny", "I prefer a partner who makes me laugh", "I prefer a partner who laughs at my humour", "Being funny is a masculine trait".

Participants were then asked to choose the statement that they agreed with: "Men are funnier than women", "Men and women are equally funny", or "Women are funnier than men", and to select which of the following statements were true about themselves: "I have more male friends than female friends", "I have an equal number of male and female friends", or "I have more female friends than male friends".
We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions (if any), all manipulations, and all measures in the study.

We also included random intercepts for nationality, ethnicity, sexual orientation, and the source of recruitment.
A significance threshold of α = .05 was used for all analyses.
Exploratory analyses examined whether perceived personal characteristics of the speaker varied as a function of apparent voice gender, original voice gender, and the gender of the participant.
A 3-way ANOVA was conducted for each characteristic (masculinity, confidence, attractiveness, warmth, competence, and charisma).
Significant ANOVA main effects were followed up using Tukey's HSD.
We note that only male and female participants were retained in these analyses due to insufficient sample size in the other gender categories.
In our main preregistered analysis, we investigated whether there was a main effect of the apparent gender of the voice on funniness ratings, i.e.
Are jokes told by a male voice funnier than jokes told by a female voice?

While controlling for participant gender, an interaction between the gender of the participant, the apparent gender of the voice, and the gender of the original voice, we found no significant difference in the funniness ratings of jokes told by apparently male and female voices, γ(SE) = -0.03(0.08), t(942.20)= -0.32, p = .745, 95% CI = [-0.19, 0.13].

text.text: We found no evidence of such an interaction between the gender of the participant and the apparent gender of the voice on ratings of funniness (γ(SE) = -0.06(0.13), t(941.93)= -0.49, p = .622, 95% CI = [-0.31, 0.19]).
That is, there was no gender difference in the tendency to find jokes told by male or female voices funnier.
We also found no evidence of a difference in funniness when jokes were originally voiced by a male or female AI voice, γ(SE) = -0.02(0.06), t(938.73)= -0.30, p = .762, 95% CI = [-0.14, 0.10].
We found that on average, men rated jokes 0.39 units (out of 7) funnier than women, γ(SE) = 0.39(0.09), t(945.52)= 4.23, p < .001, 95% CI = [0.21, 0.57].

We did not find any evidence for interactions or main effects within any of the three models except for a significant main effect of participant gender, such that on average, men gave higher funniness ratings to jokes than women (see Supplementary materials for full results).
There were significant differences between men and women on various attitudes relating to humour (Table 3).

text.text: Preregistered exploratory analyses were used to investigate whether the apparent voice gender affected perceived characteristics relating to the speaker (warmth, charisma, competence, confidence, and attractiveness), while accounting for participant gender, original voice gender, and their interactions.

In all, we only found a consistent main effect of apparent gender of the voice for perceived confidence; a male-sounding was perceived as significantly more confident than a female-sounding voice (M D = 0.18, F(1, 923) = 5.35, p = .021).

There was a significant main effect of apparent gender on ratings of charisma (F(1,923) = 17.31, p < .001), but this difference was explained by a significant interaction between the apparent and original gender of the voice.

text.text: A male voice transformed to a female voice was rated significantly less charismatic than the untransformed male voice (M D = 0.69, p adj < .001) while there was no significant difference between the female to male transformed voice and the untransformed female voice (p adj = .700).

text.text: There were no other significant main effects for the apparent gender of the voice for warmth, competence, and attractiveness ratings (p ≥ .098) (full details are reported in the Supplementary materials).

In a large sample (n = 966), we found strong evidence that jokes delivered by an apparently male voice were rated as no funnier than jokes delivered by an apparently female voice, even when controlling for the delivery of the jokes.

Most men (65%) and women (79%) in our sample agreed that "men and women are equally funny" in contrast to past findings (Caldwell & Wojtach, 2019; Hooper et al., 2016; Mickes et al., 2012), though there was still a general tendency for men (33%) and women (10%) to agree that "men funnier than women".
text.formatted: Most men (65%) and women (79%) in our sample agreed that "men and women are equally funny" in contrast to past findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Caldwell & Wojtach, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Hooper et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Mickes et al., 2012)</ref>, though there was still a general tendency for men (33%) and women (10%) to agree that "men funnier than women".

text.text: Also, participants' gender and the proportion of male friends they had were independently associated with agreement that "being funny is a masculine trait".
Finally, our study demonstrates that using an AI speech-to-speech transformation can successfully manipulate the apparent gender of a voice while controlling for delivery.
Much research has focussed on whether men and women have different humour production ability (e.g. Greengross et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Much research has focussed on whether men and women have different humour production ability (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Greengross et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Other studies have found that individuals misattribute the authorship of funny cartoon captions to male authors and unfunny captions to female authors (Hooper et al., 2016; Mickes et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Other studies have found that individuals misattribute the authorship of funny cartoon captions to male authors and unfunny captions to female authors <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hooper et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Mickes et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: However, no studies have explicitly tested whether the same humorous material and delivery is regarded funnier when it is spoken by a man compared to a woman.
Our large study is the first to examine this problem while controlling for joke delivery.

Asking participants to rate the funniness of audio jokes allows for assessment of humour perception more in line with how humour is typically consumed interpersonally or through the media, compared with past humour studies (e.g. cartoon captioning).
In the current study, we successfully manipulated the apparent gender of the voice delivering the joke while controlling for both the content and delivery of humour.
There was no evidence of an interaction between the apparent gender and original gender of the voice on ratings of voice masculinity.
In other words, specific gender cues of the original speaker were not retained when voices were transformed to the opposite gender (Figure 1).
text.formatted: In other words, specific gender cues of the original speaker were not retained when voices were transformed to the opposite gender (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: A neutral statement originally delivered by a male voice (Chris) was rated more masculine than a statement originally delivered by a female voice (Matilda), indicating that delivery alone affects the perceived masculinity of a voice.
We believe that using AI speech-to-speech transformations is an effective way to manipulate gender while controlling for the delivery of speech.

Given that variation in speech delivery can affect the perceived voice masculinity, past studies using confederates to deliver humorous content may be confounded by differences in delivery rather than humour content alone (e.g. Evans et al., 2019; Langley & Shiota, 2023; Yeo et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Given that variation in speech delivery can affect the perceived voice masculinity, past studies using confederates to deliver humorous content may be confounded by differences in delivery rather than humour content alone (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Evans et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Langley & Shiota, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Yeo et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: While we report no evidence of an interaction between the original and apparent gender of the voice on ratings of vocal masculinity, our findings are limited to the voices "Chris" and "Matilda".

In the earlier stages of this study we intended to use "Rachel" to voice jokes, but we soon realised that her voice was not conducive to delivering humorous content (see amendment to preregistration).
It is also unclear as to whether other male and female voice combinations would speech-to-speech transform as well as "Chris" and "Matilda".

Furthermore, while the voices were sourced from real individuals{ElevenLabs, 2026 #378}, we did not ask participants to what extent they thought the voice was real and whether this could affect perceptions relating to gender -a human construct.
Another limitation of our study was that we only used one voice for each gender.
Voices are distinct and can vary across many dimensions (e.g. pitch, formant, timbre).
While we selected voices that we qualitatively deemed to be generic, we cannot be certain that other voices would have produced similar results.
This limitation is not dissimilar to other confederate studies that only use one confederate of each gender (e.g. Evans et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This limitation is not dissimilar to other confederate studies that only use one confederate of each gender (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Evans et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, a substantial advantage of our paradigm, which attenuates the limitation, is that we effectively performed a within-delivery manipulation, such that we could apply a different voice while ensuring the same delivery of jokes.
In addition, our use of one-line jokes may not represent typical humour that is communicated in an everyday interpersonal context.

However, these short jokes have the advantage of conveying humour quickly and with minimal context, which helps reduce any extra variability that longer jokes or anecdotes might introduce through complex scenarios or assumptions about the speaker.

We acknowledge that the jokes in our study lean toward a masculine humour style given their edgy or inappropriate content (Hofmann et al., 2020), and most of our jokes originated from male comedians (Table 1).
text.formatted: We acknowledge that the jokes in our study lean toward a masculine humour style given their edgy or inappropriate content <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Hofmann et al., 2020)</ref>, and most of our jokes originated from male comedians (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Therefore, these jokes may not be congruent with humour typically expected from womenfoot_3 .
text.formatted: Therefore, these jokes may not be congruent with humour typically expected from women<ref type="foot" target="#foot_3">foot_3</ref> .

text.text: Research in organisational contexts suggests that women who behave and communicate in gender-incongruent ways can face negative evaluations and discrimination (Evans et al., 2019; Rudman, 1998; Rudman et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Research in organisational contexts suggests that women who behave and communicate in gender-incongruent ways can face negative evaluations and discrimination <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Evans et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Rudman, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Rudman et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: However, there are also instances where women are evaluated or received more positively than men when they use humour in organisational and social contexts (Langley & Shiota, 2023; Miron-Spektor et al., 2023).
text.formatted: However, there are also instances where women are evaluated or received more positively than men when they use humour in organisational and social contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Langley & Shiota, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Miron-Spektor et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Even though our study featured primarily masculine jokes, we found that neither the apparent gender of the voice nor gender differences in the delivery of the jokes affected how funny the joke was.
We found some evidence that evaluations of speaker characteristics reflect genderrelated biases and expectations.
After accounting for original voice gender, participant gender, and possible interactions, apparently male voices were rated as significantly more confident than apparently female voices.
This pattern is consistent with gender stereotypes that associate men with more dominant traits.
However, apparent voice gender did not show consistent main effects across other assessed traits such as warmth, competence, charisma.
There was also evidence that evaluations depended on the relation between apparent gender and vocal delivery.
Gender-transformed voices were rated as less attractive than untransformed voices, and an apparently female voice was rated as less warm when it was originally delivered by a male voice.
These findings suggest that a mismatch between the apparent gender and delivery-related vocal features lead to more negative evaluations.
However, the effects varied across traits, and it remains unclear which particular features of speech produce such perceived mismatches.
For instance, originally male voices were rated as more confident than originally female voices, indicating that delivery-related characteristics also influenced evaluations.

In all, these findings highlight the value of separating apparent speaker gender from vocal delivery: comparisons between different male and female speakers cannot determine whether perceived differences reflect gendered expectations, delivery differences, or a combination of the two.

Although exploratory, the present findings suggest that listeners evaluate voices not only according to apparent gender, but also according to stylistic features of speech and the perceived congruence between these features and gendered vocal cues.
A majority of our sample believed men and women to be equally funny, though there was a general tendency to believe that "men are funnier than women".

And on average, both men and women disagreed with the statement "being funny is a masculine trait" with mean scores falling below the midpoint of4 = neutral (Table 3), though men had higher agreement compared to women (p < .001).
text.formatted: And on average, both men and women disagreed with the statement "being funny is a masculine trait" with mean scores falling below the midpoint of4 = neutral (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">3</ref>), though men had higher agreement compared to women (p < .001).

text.text: Our sample had substantively different beliefs to those reported in other studies that sampled university students from Western English-speaking countries (Hooper et al. (2016): n = 228; Mickes et al. (2012): n = 72) and Mturkers (Caldwell and Wojtach (2019): n = 369).

(2016)</ref>: n = 228; <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Mickes et al. (2012)</ref>: n = 72) and Mturkers <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Caldwell and Wojtach (2019)</ref>: n = 369).

text.text: The age of our participants did not explain our observed discrepancies; neither participant age (p = .186) nor an interaction between participant age and gender were associated with agreement of "being funny is a masculine trait" (p ≥ .227).
There was also no difference in these attitudes across our three recruitment sources (SONA, Prolific, word of mouth) (p = .128).

Participants' beliefs about which gender is the funniest and their agreement with the statement that 'being funny is a masculine trait' was not associated with the rated funniness of jokes, regardless of whether the voice was originally male or female, or whether the voice sounded male or female.

In light of our findings, it is possible that the stereotype that "men are funnier than women" and funniness being a masculine trait could be driven by other factors beyond the immediate judgement of humour.

Men report (Myers et al., 1997) and have been observed to engage in higher rates of humour attempts (Robinson & Smith-Lovin, 2001), perceive their attempts to be more humorous (Myers et al., 1997; Silvia et al., 2021), and identify as being funny more so than women (Silvia et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Men report <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Myers et al., 1997)</ref> and have been observed to engage in higher rates of humour attempts <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Robinson & Smith-Lovin, 2001)</ref>, perceive their attempts to be more humorous <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Myers et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Silvia et al., 2021)</ref>, and identify as being funny more so than women <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Silvia et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These social cues, which may not necessarily signal humour quality, could artificially inflate perceptions of funniness in men.

Our findings reinforce this idea; participants who reported predominantly male friends had a higher agreement with the statement that "being funny is a masculine trait", even when controlling for their gender.
Individuals' perceptions of humour may be influenced by those with whom they are most likely exchange humour.
Alternatively, those who believe that funniness is a masculine trait may actively choose to have more male friends (whom they would consider to be funny).

Further analyses support the idea that social exposure influences stereotype agreement; participants who were randomly assigned an apparently female voice had a significantly lower agreement with "being funny is a masculine trait" while controlling for relevant variables.
In either case, our findings indicate that gendered attitudes toward humour could be influenced by social contexts rather than biases in humour perception.
Whether there is any truth to the stereotype that "men are funnier than women" remains an unresolved problem.
Here, we found evidence that there is no difference in the funniness of jokes delivered by male voices compared to female voices.

While previous studies suggest that men outperform women on comic captioning tasks, we cannot know whether this difference generalises to a naturalistic context, and it is unclear how humour ability would be measured given the subjective and context-dependent nature of humour judgements.

Some of our secondary findings suggest that gender stereotypes around humour are associated with social exposure to individuals of a particular gender, and that the apparent gender of the voice, vocal delivery, and a combination of the two affect evaluations of speakers.
Future studies should further explore the topic in this vein.
